title.en: The Origin of Folk Stories: Crow and the Talking Cliff
title.zh: 民間故事之起源：鴉兒與會說話的峭壁

region.en: Cliff at the forks of a river (symbolic pin at Genesee River gorge, New York)
region.zh: 河流交會處的峭壁（象徵性定位於紐約州傑納西河峽谷）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 9, 'Origin of Folk Stories' (1923)

summary.en: Gaqka, the orphan called Crow and Filth-Covered-One, finds a flying canoe, homes atop a great human-faced cliff that demands tobacco and tells wonder tales for small gifts, marries a girl whose grandfather the cliff is, and is transformed through a hollow log into a handsome man - returning north to found the custom of paying a storyteller with tobacco and a trophy drawn from the pouch for every tale.
summary.zh: 被稱為鴉兒的孤兒加卡拾得會飛的獨木舟，居於一面人形巨崖之頂；崖石索要菸草，並以小禮換取奇妙故事。他娶了崖石之孫女為妻，穿過空心圓木而蛻變為俊美男子——北歸後首創以菸草與袋中信物酬謝講故事者的習俗。

sensitivity.note: Seneca storyteller-charter tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Explains the etiquette of listening and paying for oral stories.

passages.text: There was once a boy who had no home. His parents were dead, his uncles would not care for him, and the people called him Filth-Covered-One as they passed, holding their noses. He resolved to go away and become a great hunter. One night he found a canoe that shot into the air when he took the paddle, and he flew southward above the clouds and under the moon until it dropped into a river. Across the water stood a great cliff that had a face like a man, and he built a bark cabin on its top.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 97-98; not verbatim.

passages.text: The first night a voice said, 'Give me some tobacco,' and when Gaqka threw a pinch over the cliff the voice said, 'Now I will tell you a story,' and spoke from the very rock he sat on. 'It shall be the custom hereafter to present me with a small gift for my stories,' it said; 'when I announce a story you must say Nio, as I speak you must say He', and never fall asleep until I say Da'neho nigaga'is - so thus finished is the length of my story.' All winter long the young man and his bride, who knew the rock as her grandfather, heard all the wonder tales of the old days, and his pouch was filled with a trophy for every tale.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 98-100; not verbatim.

passages.text: In spring they flew the canoe north. 'Now I shall remove your clothing and take all the scars from your face and body,' said the bride, and caused him to pass through a hollow log: Gaqka emerged in the finest clothing, a handsome man. In the village he said, 'I am the boy whom you once were accustomed to call Ga'doda. I have now returned.' That night the people gathered to hear his tales, instructed to give him small presents and tobacco; he plunged his hand into the pouch, took out a trophy and told an ancient tale. That is why there are so many legends now.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 100; not verbatim.

title.en: The Forbidden Arrow and the Quilt of Men's Eyes

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

texts.period: Related in Seneca by Edward Cornplanter, translated by William Bluesky (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 10, 'The Forbidden Arrow and the Quilt of Men's Eyes' (1923)

summary.en: Twin brothers disobey their grandmother and shoot their father's forbidden arrow, pinning Driven to the earth in the north. Passing the witch women's dancing house with eyes cast down, Younger is forced at last to look on the quilt of living young men's eyes and is blinded; his wizard sons borrow a fawn's eyes, trick the witches into destroying one another, restore father and uncle's sight, and resurrect the magically slain - whose mismated limbs become the first cripples of the world.
summary.zh: 雙生兄弟違逆祖母，射出父親的禁忌之箭，把「被逐者」釘在北方大地。途中少年被迫直視巫婦以活人眼珠縫成的被子而失明；其術士之子借小鹿之眼為父復明，誘使巫婦自相殘殺，尋回父叔的眼珠，並令被魔法所殺者復生——其錯配的肢體便成為世上最早的殘疾之人。

sensitivity.note: Seneca transformation myth (Cornplanter/Bluesky, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker's own note: the orenda of twins, the magic arrow, and the resurrection with mismated limbs are recurrent Seneca motifs.

passages.text: Two twin brothers, Younger and Driven, played about two hills: Driven jumped from one summit to the other while Younger shot arrows at him in flight. Their grandmother always forbade them a certain arrow that had belonged to their father. At last they used it; the forbidden arrow pierced Driven's body and carried him northward, singing with wild-duck feathers, and Younger ran a long way to find his brother transfixed to the earth. Carrying him on his back he was warned: a house of dancing women lay ahead - 'Oh brother, cast not your eyes upon one of them!' - and beyond it the lodge where women made a quilt of young men's eyes, that live and wink as in life.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 101-102; not verbatim.

passages.text: Through the long lodge Younger kept his eyes to the ground, but at the door one woman held the quilt where he saw it: his eyes jumped out of their sockets into the quilt, and he was blind. He crept on hands and knees to a cornfield and lay there day after day until two sisters found him and carried him home, feeding him bear's oil until he grew strong; he married the younger sister, who bore twin boys, wizards who talked before they suckled and played lacrosse under the ground.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 102-104; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Father, we will go and get back your eyes,' said the sons. They borrowed a fawn's eyes (feeding her moss meanwhile), then transformed the younger into a duck at the witches' spring and leaped into a woman's body to be born of her; as a fretful child he cried for treasures until they showed him the quilt of eyes, and when the women were in the field he folded it and ran. The witches pursued him with hammers, struck and killed each other, and the boys set father and uncle's own eyes back in their sockets.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 105-107; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'We must now go and find the bones of the dead and restore them their eyes,' said the twins. They gathered the skeletons under a lodge roof of white bear skin; the wigwam quivered, and kicking over an elm as a warning the boys cried, 'The tree is falling upon you. Flee for your lives!' The living dead ran out with eyes on their skulls but no time to find their own bones: some had legs too short, some long arms and short legs - their limbs mismated. From them sprang the deformed and ugly people of today, and a great house sprang up at Last's footprints to hold them all.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 107; not verbatim.

title.en: Corn Grinder, the Grandson: The Boy Who Went South
title.zh: 磨玉米之孫：向南而行的男孩

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

texts.period: Related by Guy Miller, a Tuscarora, Jan. 1905 (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 11, 'Corn Grinder, the Grandson' (1923)

summary.en: Warned never to wander south beyond the sound of the corn grinder, the boy goes south at last, finds a lodge of giants, scalds the giant baby with soup grease and pepper, shoots the male giant dead - and learns from his grandmother that he has killed his own father. With the invisible friend Standing Cob he quests through beast-haunted forests to a cataract for the medicine roots, shoots his weeping father down from the pine where the crowd has been harvesting his wampum tears, and the whole enchanted family is restored to normal human size.
summary.zh: 男孩被告誡不得離開磨杵聲所及之地向南而行，終究南行，發現巨人一家的居所；以滾油與辛辣草戲弄巨嬰，射殺男巨人——祖母卻說他殺了親生父親。他與隱形朋友「立玉米棒」穿越野獸出沒的森林，往瀑底尋得藥根，將在松樹上哭泣（淚珠落地成貝珠）的父親射下，一家人終復為常人之形。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora-related Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Violence is folklore-trickster register, not instruction.

passages.text: In a clearing in a thick pine forest lived an old couple who talked with trees, with their grandson, whom they named Corn Grinder. 'Go east, go west, go north, but not away from the sound of the corn grinder,' they said. 'Never go south!' At twelve he knew the woods in every direction but the forbidden south, and at last resolved to disobey. He found a great bark lodge where a gigantic woman cooked corn soup and a baby lay as tall as a warrior; hiding under the bed, he was nearly crushed by the rolling infant, and ran out, skimmed a ladle of scalding grease from the soup and threw it on the baby's belly, fleeing to the woods.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 108-110; not verbatim.

passages.text: He threw pungent weeds into the soup, and the giantess sneezed until she could scarcely stand - 'Some witch must be near.' Strapping the baby to the board she sang 'Luk-ste, luk-ste, da-ja-jent' at a huge dead tree, which opened to let out a tall giant who scalded his throat on the soup and kicked the kettle flying over the trees. Corn Grinder learned the song, struck the tree himself when the sun stood high, and as the giant stormed out - 'More tricks!' - shot an arrow through his stomach. Rushing home he cried, 'Oh grandmother! I killed him, I killed him!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 110-112; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Age!' wailed the old woman. 'You have killed your father, my own son. You must go on a long journey to a high mountain and obtain certain magical roots to restore him. Why did you disobey us?' The giantess and the baby burst in to kill him; he leaped down the giantess' throat, wrenched out her heart, and killed the infant, then set out with his invisible friend Da-ga-ga-we-so-da-de, Standing Cob. At a clearing near the mountain a multitude was shooting at a creature in the topmost pine whose tears of wampum dropped at every arrow. 'Stop!' said Cob. 'That is your father up there. Hurry and get the medicine.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 112-114; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a deep rift at the foot of a cataract they found the wonderful plant, which soared upward until Cob leaped and caught it by the roots. Corn Grinder chewed the roots and rubbed his saliva over his body, clothing and arrows, and felt new vigor. At the great pine he spat on his arrows, rubbed the roots in his hair and shot: the creature vanished, and both boys were pulled through the air like the wind, dropping at the doorway of a new lodge where a woman sang to a baby - the same mother, father and child he had killed, each now grown smaller. 'I am your brother,' said the baby. 'I am your father,' said the man. 'Come, let us eat!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 114-115; not verbatim.
